children: The World Gold Council reports a 15 per cent year-on-year decline in Indian jewellery demand in the second quarter of 2026, even as the value of jewellery demand rose 34 per cent

As India enters the festive season, gold remains firmly embedded in household buying plans, but what consumers are buying is changing. A year-long surge in prices has made traditional heavy jewellery increasingly difficult to afford, pushing buyers towards lighter pieces and old-gold exchanges, while those looking at gold primarily as an investment are increasingly turning to exchange-traded funds (ETFs), coins and digital gold.

Domestic gold prices have climbed around 60 per cent in a year, from roughly Rs 98,000 to around Rs 1.57 lakh per 10 grams. The rally has been driven by the global rise in gold prices, a weaker rupee, which is trading around Rs 95.6 to the US dollar, and an increase in import duty from 6 per cent to 15 per cent in April.

The impact is already visible in jewellery volumes. Gold sales volumes during Ganesh Chaturthi fell around 15 per cent, although the decline in volumes has not translated into a comparable fall in the value of purchases.

“The 60 per cent year-on-year surge has reshaped the cart, not killed the intent,” said Nikunj Saraf, CEO, Choice Wealth. “Buyers are trading down in weight but not walking away: lighter, lower-carat and studded pieces, more old-gold exchange to fund new purchases, and a clear tilt towards coins and bars.”

This shift is creating a divergence between the amount of gold consumers buy and the money they spend on it. Prasanna Pathak, Deputy CEO, The Wealth Company Mutual Fund, said “Consumers are increasingly opting for lighter-weight, lower-carat and lower-making-charge jewellery, with old-gold exchanges helping bridge the affordability gap.”

The World Gold Council reported a 15 per cent year-on-year decline in Indian jewellery demand in the second quarter of 2026, even as the value of jewellery demand rose 34 per cent. The divergence suggests that elevated prices are changing the composition of demand rather than eliminating the underlying appetite for gold.
Investment Gold Gains Ground

The bigger structural shift may be taking place outside jewellery stores. Gold ETFs received net inflows of Rs 1,559 crore in July, before inflows rose 67 per cent month-on-month to Rs 2,597 crore in August. Gold ETF assets under management (AUM) reached around Rs 1.91 lakh crore in August.

“Consumers are now keeping jewellery and investment separate,” said Akshat Garg, Head, Research & Product, Choice Wealth. He also pointed to a more than doubling of digital gold purchases year-on-year in August, alongside a 58 per cent decline in gold imports to USD 2.3 billion.

Sarvam Goel, Founder, Pocketful, said the shift towards financial forms of gold is becoming increasingly visible. “People now want the savings side of gold in simpler forms, easier to buy in small amounts, hold and sell,” he said.

Gold ETFs attracted roughly Rs 41,500 crore between January and August, according to Goel, almost matching the inflows recorded through the whole of the previous year. Digital gold purchases have also averaged around Rs 2,500 crore a month since June.
“Jewellery isn’t going away. It will increasingly be bought for weddings and wearing, while savings move to coins, ETFs and digital gold,” Goel said.

Adil Chacko, Executive Director, Anand Rathi Wealth, sees the same trend in physical investment demand. Gold ETF demand reached a record 24 tonnes in the first half of 2026, up 163 per cent year-on-year, while holdings rose to 119 tonnes and AUM reached Rs 1.7 lakh crore. Bar and coin demand also reached 113 tonnes, the highest level in 13 years.

“If investors have the objective of owning gold as an investment, there is no need to buy a piece of jewellery, pay making charges and then worry about storage or selling it later,” Chacko said. “ETFs and other financial forms of gold make it easier to buy smaller amounts and track the investment.”
High prices may change the demand mix

The shift could become more pronounced if gold prices remain elevated for an extended period. There is no single price level at which jewellery demand becomes a problem for the broader gold market, said Vandana Bharti, Head of Commodity Research, SMC Global Securities.

“The more important factor is the duration of elevated prices and their impact on affordability and household incomes,” Bharti said. “If prices remain high for an extended period, jewellery volumes can remain under pressure, but investment demand can partly compensate through bars, coins and financial products.”
India’s demand mix is already reflecting that transition. In the first quarter of 2026, bar-and-coin demand almost matched jewellery demand, according to Bharti.
For the festive season, therefore, the question may not simply be whether Indians will buy gold. It is increasingly about which form of gold they choose to buy.

Jewellery remains tied to weddings, traditions and consumption, while the savings component of India’s centuries-old gold habit is steadily moving towards products that can be bought in smaller quantities, held more easily and traded without the costs attached to physical jewellery.
Krishna Chourasia
BW Reporters The author is a Correspondent at BW Businessworld.
